morningLine: Arcade hits travel to rival machines, Big Blue brings the mainframe to the desk, and DEC puts VAX power into a microcomputer.

lead.headline: Atari Takes Its Games to Rival Machines
lead.dek: The Atarisoft label carries arcade names beyond Atari hardware as the home-game business searches for software revenue.
body: Atari is loosening the bond between its famous games and its own machines. A New York Times report on October 27 described new Atari titles made to fit competing home systems, turning the company’s arcade catalog into a software line that could reach players well beyond the Atari 2600 and Atari computers.

The Atarisoft label gave the strategy a bright retail identity. Platform-coded packages—surviving Apple II editions, for example, wear red—let shoppers spot the version for their machine while the Atari name and familiar coin-op artwork supplied the attraction. The box, rather than the console, became the company’s new front door.

That shift matters in a difficult year for video games. Instead of demanding that a household buy Atari hardware before buying Atari entertainment, the publisher could earn from owners of rival computers and consoles. Arcade properties could be translated, repackaged and placed on many more store shelves.

The conversions will still be judged machine by machine: controls, graphics and sound differ sharply across home platforms. Yet the business signal is already clear. A great game can travel, and in the crowded autumn of 1983 Atari is betting that its software names may range farther than any single box beneath the television.

stories.headline: IBM Links the PC Desk to the Mainframe
stories.dek: The 3270 PC and XT/370 join local work with corporate host access.
body: IBM is bringing two worlds onto one desktop. The 3270 Personal Computer combines PC-class local processing with access to IBM 4300- and 3080-series hosts, and was described as handling as many as seven applications concurrently, four supplied by host systems.

The Personal Computer XT/370 goes further, fitting an XT with three specialized boards so VM/370 applications can be processed locally. Its hardware includes terminal emulation, 524K of added real memory, an Intel 8087 and two Motorola 68000-family processors, with as much as 4MB of virtual memory.

For corporate buyers, the promise is continuity rather than rebellion: familiar languages and procedures from the machine room, paired with spreadsheets and other personal work at the employee’s desk.

stories.headline: DEC Shrinks 32-Bit VAX Power Into a Microcomputer
stories.dek: MicroVAX I points departmental and technical computing toward smaller packages.
body: Digital Equipment Corporation has unveiled the MicroVAX I, described in the October 24 Computerworld as the first micro-based implementation of DEC’s 32-bit VAX architecture. DEC rated it at roughly 35 percent of the processing power of a VAX-11/780 and support for as many as eight users.

The system is aimed at industrial control as well as business and scientific work. MicroVMS, the real-time VAXELN environment and the Unix-compatible Ultrix accompanied the hardware news, signaling that the smaller VAX is intended as a platform rather than a single-purpose curiosity.

stories.headline: FBI Seizes Gear in Multicity Hacker Inquiry
stories.dek: Unauthorized access becomes a national law-enforcement and privacy story.
body: The FBI has seized equipment belonging to 15 alleged computer hackers in 13 cities, Computerworld reports. The sweep shows how quickly remote access and electronic trespass have moved from hobbyist circles into a coordinated federal investigation.

The same issue gives prominent attention to computer matching and privacy concerns. Together, the stories place two sides of connected computing in view: outsiders reaching systems without permission, and institutions combining personal records with growing power.
